raw_text:
**Peripartum cardiomyopathy**

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting as heart failure with left ventricular systolic dysfunction toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, without another identifiable cause [1–4]. Contemporary definitions usually require a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) below 45%, although left ventricular dilatation is not mandatory [4]. The syndrome was clinically delineated in early series that emphasized its postpartum presentation and variable natural history [2], and subsequent reviews have reframed PPCM as a heterogeneous disorder at the intersection of pregnancy biology, vascular injury, genetic susceptibility, and conventional heart failure [5–8].

Reported incidence varies markedly by geography, ascertainment, and population. US administrative studies suggest increasing recognition over time, with disproportionate burden among Black women [9–11]. European population-based data show lower incidence but similar dependence of prognosis on presenting LVEF [12]. In Nigeria and other high-burden regions, PPCM may be far more common, with presentations often advanced and complicated by right ventricular dysfunction, thrombus, or stroke [13]. Established risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, pre-eclampsia, and African ancestry [10,11,14]. The strong epidemiologic link with pre-eclampsia has supported a vascular model of disease rather than a purely hemodynamic one [14].

Pathobiology is multifactorial. Experimental work identified oxidative stress–mediated cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa antiangiogenic fragment, producing endothelial injury and cardiomyocyte dysfunction [15]. A complementary angiogenic-imbalance model showed that excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1), particularly in pre-eclampsia or multiple gestation, can stress the maternal heart when cardiomyocyte angiogenic reserve is impaired [16]. In the IPAC biomarker cohort, higher sFlt1 correlated with worse symptoms and adverse events, whereas relaxin-2 was associated with early recovery [17]. Genetics also contributes: truncating variants, especially in TTN, are enriched in PPCM and overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy [18], with broader sequencing confirming a genetic and phenotypic continuum in a subset of patients [19].

Clinically, PPCM may be missed because dyspnea, edema, fatigue, and orthopnea overlap with normal late pregnancy and puerperium. Red flags include progressive dyspnea, pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, persistent tachycardia, elevated natriuretic peptides, new murmurs, arrhythmias, thromboembolism, or cardiogenic shock. Echocardiography is central for diagnosis, quantifying LVEF, chamber size, right ventricular function, valvular regurgitation, pulmonary pressures, and intracardiac thrombus [4,7]. In the North American IPAC study, most women improved, but 13% had death, mechanical support/transplantation, or persistent severe cardiomyopathy at 1 year; lower initial LVEF and greater LV dilatation predicted poorer recovery [20]. The ESC EORP registry confirmed wide global variation in presentation and care, emphasizing the need for early diagnosis and specialized cardio-obstetric management [21]. Cardiac magnetic resonance may assist when myocarditis, infarction, infiltrative disease, or thrombus is suspected; emerging data suggest CMR markers may refine risk stratification [29].

Management depends on pregnancy status and severity. Acute therapy addresses congestion, oxygenation, blood pressure, arrhythmia, and end-organ perfusion. During pregnancy, fetal safety limits use of renin–angiotensin system blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and some anticoagulants; hydralazine–nitrate combinations, beta-1 selective blockers, cautious diuresis, and anticoagulation when indicated are commonly used [25–27]. After delivery, guideline-directed therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction should be instituted and titrated, including ACE inhibitor or ARB/ARNI when compatible with lactation choices, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, diuretics, and anticoagulation for severe LV dysfunction or thrombus risk [25–27]. Arrhythmia surveillance is important, but permanent defibrillator decisions are usually deferred for several months because recovery is common; wearable defibrillators may bridge selected high-risk patients [28]. Fulminant PPCM requires rapid transfer to centers capable of inotropes, temporary mechanical circulatory support, durable LV assist devices, transplantation, and high-risk obstetric care [7,26].

Bromocriptine, which suppresses prolactin, remains the most discussed disease-specific therapy. Small randomized and prospective studies suggested improved recovery when added to standard heart failure therapy [22,23], and meta-analytic data support possible benefit but with limitations in trial size, heterogeneity, and antithrombotic co-management [24]. If used, concomitant anticoagulation is generally recommended because bromocriptine and severe LV dysfunction may increase thrombotic risk [22–24]. Decisions about breastfeeding should be individualized, balancing maternal heart failure severity, desire to breastfeed, medication compatibility, and local expertise.

Follow-up should include serial echocardiography, medication optimization, contraception counseling, and shared decision-making about future pregnancy. Persistent LVEF reduction is the strongest contraindication to subsequent pregnancy; even recovered women retain relapse risk and need preconception evaluation, close surveillance, and multidisciplinary care [26,30]. PPCM therefore demands prompt recognition, exclusion of mimics, aggressive heart failure care adapted to pregnancy and lactation, and long-term cardiovascular follow-up.
